items.title: Red Holloway interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995
items.q: And Milt Fillius asked us to ask you about Central Avenue

ctx.x: Ahhh, listen, you know what? I don’t know. There was a friend of mine — in Los Angeles there’s is a young fellow, he says, “He sounds like you.” I said, “Well no, he doesn’t have the sound.” He said, “No, but the stuff that he plays and the phrasing,” he said Ricky Woodard. I can’t see it, but I listen to Ricky and there is this saxophone player, what’s his name — Wilbur Brown. Now Wilbur Brown is a hell of a saxophone player. He lives in L.A. But he says, “Ricky Woodard sounds like you.” I say, “Well not for…

I wanted to ask you about, you know there’s different places in the country where ideas seem to gel collectively for musicians. And Milt Fillius asked us to ask you about Central Avenue, and the things that were going on and the people that you played with.

Well, actually I never played on Central Avenue, but I was very aware of it. See like I say I was raised in Chicago. When I got to California, I got to California in the 60s, like in ‘67. But I had been to California in 1962 and ‘63 with Lloyd Price’s band. But I never got on Central Avenue when it really was Central Avenue, you know, when it really had a lot of like Central Avenue Breakdown by Lionel Hampton, you know? In fact I was in New York before I got to California I went to New York in 1946 when I was in…
